content.thinking:
I notice the flag was switched on at 10:01:33Z, but the actual onset appears earlier at 09:56 with G971b ramping and Gce95 coming online at 09:57 — so I need to be careful to date each change by its own recorded instant, not by an effect that happened before it.

So the honest framing is: the provider's record dates the flag switch at 10:01:33, well after the onset at 09:56, which means the record itself doesn't explain the gap — I shouldn't claim the flag flipped at 09:56 just because that's when the logs show it evaluating on. C1's claim that it switched "at the onset" is the candidate's framing, not what the record shows, so I'll flag that discrepancy explicitly. I'm also ruling out other candidate changes since there were no deploys and only this one flag history entry — any earlier change gets ruled out only if the service was already measured healthy with it in place.

I can also rule out the running revision as the trigger since metrics were healthy before onset with that revision deployed, and healthy again after the flag was reverted without the revision changing. And those pre-onset ClientDisconnected errors look like baseline noise rather than a contributing cause, since they occurred before onset while the service was still healthy.

Now I'm tracing the causal chain: shoppers hit failures on account pages (Gbac1 error spike, G5309 errors, AL1 alert), caused by ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47 starting at 09:56 with no such errors beforehand. That code path only executes when the monthly-spend-feature flag is on — logs show it flipping on around 09:56-09:57 (G971b, Gce95) after being off before (G7e5d), and turning it back off cleared the errors, which lines up with the admin's flag change recorded in the provider history.

I check why the division by zero happens: per the source reading (F1, unverified), the code divides by this month's purchase count, which is zero for shoppers without purchases this month — consistent with the G5309 error. Since this step rests on an unverified reading, it still counts as reaching a cause. I still need to dig into why the admin turned the flag on in the first place, since stopping at "a person did it" isn't sufficient.

I'm also looking at what let the harm happen: no visible test coverage for the zero-purchase case, and the flag went from a partial rollout (120/80) to fully on within about a minute rather than ramping gradually. That suggests two possible fixes — adding CI tests for this edge case, and requiring the flag-on code path to run in tests before it can go live in production.

I'm also weighing whether the ramp needed an automatic halt tied to rising error rates, since exposure could've stayed limited to the partial share if a guard had triggered. As for paging, nobody was paged on-call, but since the automated detection system caught it quickly anyway, that doesn't seem like a factor that would have shortened or prevented the incident, so I'm inclined to leave it out of the lessons.

I'm also noting a discrepancy: the flag provider's audit history records the toggle switching after the incident started, but the evaluation logs show it was already on from 09:56 — these two sources don't line up. This isn't itself a contributing factor since it wouldn't have changed the incident timeline, but it's a real investigation gap worth flagging as an action item to reconcile the provider's audit timestamps with the evaluation logs.

Now I'm drafting additional action items: a pre-enable check running the account page test suite before monthly-spend-feature can go live in production, auto-revert on flag ramps when error rates spike, the process item to investigate the timestamp discrepancy, and possibly a detection item for alerting on new exception types like ZeroDivisionError on the account page.

For contributing factors, I'm noting there was no test exercising the monthly figure for a shopper with zero purchases while the flag was on, and the flag ramped from partial to full within roughly a minute without any guard halting on errors — I can describe this as happening "within the next minute" since I can't pin down exact numbers from the overlapping timestamp ranges. I'm also noting that Argus reverted the flag after being called in, trying to pin down the exact timing of that action.

For went_wrong, the real gap seems to be that nobody was paged — there's no on-call incident linked to this alert, so no one was notified while it was active. I'm debating whether to flag the mismatch between the change record's timestamp and actual onset as a discrepancy, likely logging it under assumptions as well as a separate issue, and deciding whether "no person was paged" warrants its own action item.

For got_lucky, I don't see anything worth noting — the fix was reversible, not luck, and unaffected shoppers were more fault than fortune, so I'll leave it empty. For still_at_risk, I'll note that the division-by-zero bug remains live in the running code, so re-enabling the monthly-spend feature would reproduce the same account-page failures for shoppers with no purchases this month, based on F1 and G5309. For root cause, I'm framing it as: with the monthly-spend-feature on, the account page divides total spend by item count for the month, which is zero for shoppers with no purchases, triggering a ZeroDivisionError.

I want to phrase the plain-words cause without using "zero" directly — something like "divide by the number of purchases, which fails when there were none." The symptom becomes "shoppers' account pages failed to load," and I should avoid stray numbers except for identifiers like the filename/line reference, which is fine since it's a name, not a count.

I'm noting some underlying assumptions to flag: that the flag logs match actual rollout timing, that the divide-by-zero really traces back to the unrun code, and that the observed failure rate (14 log lines against error rate) might be sampled rather than exhaustive. For ruling things out, I confirm no deploys happened the day before onset, and that the service only recovered once the flag was reverted on the same running revision — which points squarely at the flag change rather than a deploy or revision shift.

Also noting ClientDisconnected errors were already present at baseline before onset, so they're not the culprit, and that only a single flag change (P1) occurred around that time.

action_items.item: Before monthly-spend-feature can be switched on in production, require the account page tests to pass with the flag on, including a shopper with no purchases this month.
Make flag rollouts halt and turn the flag back off automatically when the account page error rate rises during the rollout.
Find out why the flag provider's history dates the monthly-spend-feature switch at {P1.1} when the service's logs show the flag evaluating on from {G971b.1}.
Page the on-call engineer when HighErrorRate fires on io-shop.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed. The share of requests that failed rose from {errors_before} before the onset to {errors_at_worst} at worst, and the service's own warning for account page errors peaked at {Gbac1.7}. Failed requests are pages shoppers could not see.

Account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError: division by zero at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47. These errors start at {G5309.3}, in the minute of the onset. Before the onset the only failures logged were shoppers closing the connection.

ruled_out.what: A deploy or release: none came back for the day before the onset.
The revision running on every replica, which the history does not name: it stayed in place after the flag was turned off, and the service was measured back to normal.
The ClientDisconnected failures: they were already logged before the onset, while account pages were at their usual error rate.
Any other flag change: the provider's history shows only the one change to monthly-spend-feature.

causal_chain.step: The failing code runs when monthly-spend-feature is on. Before the onset every evaluation of the flag came back off. At {G971b.1} some evaluations came back on, and from {Gce95.4} all of them did. Turning the flag off brought the service back to normal with nothing else changed. The flag provider's history records only one switch-on, by admin at {P1.1}, which is after the onset. The record does not show why the logs show the flag evaluating on before the time the provider records.

Code-Fix read the source but did not run it, so this step is unverified. Its reading is that with the flag on, render_spend_summary calls average_spend_per_item_this_month. That function divides the month's total by the number of items bought this month, which is empty for a shopper who has bought before but not this month. That fits the division by zero the logs show at spend_summary.py:47.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Turning on a new monthly spending summary made the account page divide by the number of items a shopper had bought this month, and that fails for shoppers who had bought nothing this month.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that runs the monthly spend path with the flag on for a shopper who has no purchases this month. Code-Fix's draft adds such tests.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The division by zero could have been caught before the flag reached any shopper.

contributing_factors.factor: The flag went from some evaluations on at {G971b.1} to all of them on from {Gce95.4}. No guard was seen that halts a flag rollout when account page errors rise.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The rollout could have stopped or reversed while only part of the traffic had the flag on, which would have limited the failures and shortened them.

went_well: Argus turned monthly-spend-feature off {T18.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, and the service was measured back to normal from {T20.2}.
Turning the flag off could be undone and touched nothing else, so the fault was contained without a deploy.
Code-Fix opened a draft fix with tests {T23.1 - T22.1} after the incident was marked mitigated.
went_wrong: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to the alert, so no person was told while account pages were failing.
The only flag change in the provider's history is dated after the onset, so the record of changes did not line up with when the failures began.

input.root_cause: With monthly-spend-feature on, the account page works out a shopper's average spend per item this month by dividing the month's total by the number of items bought this month. For a shopper with no purchases this month that count is empty, so the request raised ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47 and the page failed. The log lines show the division by zero at that line. The part about the empty count of this month's items comes from Code-Fix's reading of the source, which nothing ran.
input.still_at_risk: The division by zero is still in the code the service runs, so switching monthly-spend-feature back on would make account pages fail again for shoppers with no purchases this month.
input.symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
